title: New School Food Rules: What's Changing in Your Cafeteria?
summary: Imagine asking your lunch lady to make a TikTok recipe. That's what kids in one Pennsylvania school district are doing! But big changes are coming to school cafeterias across the U.S. In January, the government released new dietary guidelines (rules about what we should eat) as part of the Make America Healthy Again plan. They want schools to serve less processed food (food with lots of added stuff) and more protein like meat and eggs. But here's the problem: protein is expensive. Schools get about $4.60 from the government for each free lunch they serve. That money has to pay for food, workers, and kitchen equipment. Some schools already struggle to make ends meet. The new rules also cut funding for buying local food from farmers. Nichole Taylor, who runs food services in Great Valley School District, supports the idea of healthier food but worries about the cost. "We want to follow the guidelines, but we also have to be realistic," she said. The government says it will take a few years to update the rules. Meanwhile, schools are already cutting added sugar in some foods. What do you think—would you eat more veggies if your cafeteria had them?
why_it_matters: The food your school serves might change—fewer sugary treats and more meats, but if costs go up, you could see fewer choices or higher lunch prices.

background_read: School lunches in the U.S. have been supported by the National School Lunch Program since 1946, which helps feed about 30 million children every school day.
President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) launched the 'Make America Healthy Again' plan to push for better nutrition and less processed food.

In the past, schools had to follow rules called 'dietary guidelines' that tell them how much fruit, vegetables, and whole grains to serve, but now the focus is shifting to protein and cutting added sugar.
Article_Structure: WHO: Kids in Pennsylvania schools, lunch ladies, and Nichole Taylor, who directs food services for Great Valley School District.
WHAT: New government dietary guidelines want cafeterias to cut processed food and add more protein, but schools face money problems because protein costs more.
WHERE: School cafeterias across the United States, with an example from a school district in Pennsylvania.
WHY: The change is part of the 'Make America Healthy Again' plan to improve kids' health, but the challenge is that funding was cut for local food and the new rules may strain tight budgets.

perspectives.description: Many people, including Nichole Taylor, think healthier meals with less sugar will help students grow strong, think clearly, and learn better.
Some school officials are worried because protein is expensive and the government is not giving extra money, so they might struggle to pay for everything else like kitchen staff and equipment.
